content: Fraxinus is a genus of flowering plants that belongs to the family Oleaceae, which also includes olives and lilacs. This genus comprises between 45 and 65 species, most of which are medium to large deciduous trees, although a few subtropical species are evergreen. The common English name for these trees, ash, originates from the Old English word æsc, while the Latin-derived generic name Fraxinus also means spear in both languages. The leaves of ash trees are typically arranged in opposite pairs, though occasionally they are found in whorls of three. Most species have pinnately compound leaves, although a few species have simple leaves. The seeds of ash trees, commonly referred to as keys or helicopter seeds, are a type of fruit known as a samara. It is important to note that rowans or mountain ashes, despite their similar appearance, are not true ash trees and belong to the genus Sorbus. Selected Species of Fraxinus Some notable species of Fraxinus include: Fraxinus americana (White Ash or Autumn Purple Ash) Fraxinus caroliniana (Carolina Ash) Fraxinus nigra (Black Ash) Fraxinus pennsylvanica (Green Ash) Fraxinus profunda (Pumpkin Ash) Fraxinus quadrangulata (Blue Ash) Fraxinus excelsior (European Ash) Fraxinus ornus (Manna Ash or Flowering Ash) Fraxinus chinensis (Chinese Ash or Korean Ash) Fraxinus mandschurica (Manchurian Ash) Fraxinus velutina (Velvet Ash or Arizona Ash) Fraxinus angustifolia (Narrow-leafed Ash) Ecological Role Ash trees serve as a food source for the larvae of certain species of Lepidoptera, which include butterflies and moths. These insects rely on ash trees as part of their life cycle. Threats to Ash Trees The emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis), a wood-boring beetle native to eastern Asia, was accidentally introduced to North America in the late 1980s or early 1990s through solid wood packing materials. This invasive species has caused the death of tens of millions of ash trees across 15 U.S. states and parts of Ontario, Canada. It poses a significant threat to approximately 7 billion ash trees in North America. Efforts are underway to explore biological control methods, including the use of three native Asian wasp species that are natural predators of the emerald ash borer. Public awareness campaigns emphasize the importance of not transporting unfinished wood products, such as firewood, to help slow the spread of this destructive pest. Uses of Ash Wood Ash wood is highly valued for its strength, density, toughness, and elasticity. It is commonly used in the production of bows, tool handles, baseball bats, and hurleys, as well as other applications requiring durability and resilience. Ash wood is also a popular material for electric guitar bodies, where it is prized for its bright tone and sustain, and is occasionally used for acoustic guitar bodies. Additionally, it is used in the construction of drum shells and interior joinery. Ash veneers are frequently employed in the manufacture of office furniture. However, ash wood is not widely used outdoors due to its low durability when in contact with the ground, as the heartwood typically decays within five years. Woodworkers appreciate ash for its excellent finishing qualities and ease of use with nails, screws, and glue. Historically, ash wood was used in the structural components of early automobiles, particularly in frames designed to flex as part of the suspension system. The Morgan Motor Company in Great Britain continues to manufacture sports cars with ash wood frames. Early aviation pioneers also utilized ash wood in aircraft construction. Furthermore, ash wood is an excellent choice for firewood and is often used for barbecuing or smoking food. The two most economically significant species for wood production are White Ash (Fraxinus americana) in North America and European Ash (Fraxinus excelsior) in Europe. Green Ash (Fraxinus pennsylvanica) is widely planted as a street tree in the United States. The inner bark of Blue Ash (Fraxinus quadrangulata) has historically been used as a source of blue dye. Cultural Significance In Greek mythology, the Meliae were nymphs associated with ash trees, possibly the Manna Ash (Fraxinus ornus), similar to how dryads were linked to oak trees. These nymphs are mentioned in Hesiod's Theogony. The ash tree produces a sugary substance that may have been fermented to create the Norse Mead of Inspiration. In Norse mythology, the World Tree Yggdrasil is often identified as an ash tree, and the first man, Ask, was said to have been formed from an ash tree. In European folklore, ash leaves or branches were believed to repel snakes, and in Irish tradition, shadows cast by ash trees were thought to harm crops. In Cheshire, England, ash was believed to cure warts or rickets, while in Sussex, the ash and elm trees were nicknamed Widow Makers due to their tendency to drop large branches without warning.
